Newly hatched chicks of the White-breasted waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) emerge from the egg at a mass of 19.6 grams [Ww0 = 19.6 grams], a modest initial wet weight indicative of a semi-precocial developmental strategy. The incubation period, measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], lasts exactly 20 days [ab = 20 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other small rallids. Following hatching, the altricial nestlings remain in the nest, dependent on biparental provisioning during a rapid growth phase. The time from birth to fledging, also recorded at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], is a remarkably brief 9 days [tx = 9 days], after which the precocial chicks can swim and forage alongside their parents. This accelerated developmental timeline is likely an adaptation to the species’ typical wetland habitats, which are often subject to fluctuating water levels that could threaten ground-based nests. Comparable developmental rates have been documented in the closely related Baillon’s crake, though the latter species tends to show a slightly longer nestling period. The energetic demands of such rapid growth are substantial and are met through intensive feeding by both adult birds.

Sexual maturity in Amaurornis phoenicurus is attained relatively quickly for a bird of its body size, with individuals reaching puberty at 150 days after birth [tp = 150 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This relatively early onset of reproductive capability is consistent with the species’ high intrinsic rate of increase and its classification as an r-selected strategist within its family. The age at first reproduction, representing the time from birth to the first successful brood, is considerably longer, being recorded at 2.6 years since birth [tR = 2.6 years since birth] when maintained at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This delay between achieving puberty and actually breeding is a critical period during which young birds must establish a territory, form a pair bond, and acquire the necessary foraging skills to sustain the high energetic costs of egg production and chick rearing. Field observations in southern India confirm that most first-year birds do not breed, instead remaining in non-territorial flocks until their second year. This pre-reproductive period effectively serves as a buffer, allowing individuals to accumulate sufficient body reserves to invest in their first clutch, which typically numbers between 4 and 9 eggs.

The maximum reproductive rate of the White-breasted waterhen is defined by a combination of clutch size and laying frequency. Females produce a clutch of 4 to 9 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 4 to 9 eggs], with the modal value being around 6 or 7 eggs in most populations studied. Under optimal conditions and at the species’ preferred thermal environment of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], individuals can achieve a reproductive frequency of approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year], a figure derived from the daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.178 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.178 eggs per day]. This rate facilitates an intense breeding schedule enabled by the short incubation and nestling periods described earlier, as well as by the species’ flexible breeding season, which spans the monsoon and post-monsoon months in much of its Asian range. Investment in multiple broods is typical, and renesting following predation is common and swift. The trade-off between clutch size and chick quality is apparent, as broods from larger clutches tend to exhibit slightly lower fledging success due to competition for food. This high annual output, combined with a relatively long breeding lifespan, contributes substantially to the species’ demographic success.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in Amaurornis phoenicurus, with females attaining a maximum ultimate wet weight of 203 grams [Wwi = 203 grams] and males reaching a substantially larger 299 grams [Wwi = 299 grams]. This 32% difference in adult body mass between the sexes is among the most extreme recorded within the family Rallidae. The larger males are better equipped for territorial defense and aggressive encounters with conspecifics, whereas the smaller female body mass may reduce the energetic costs of egg production and allow for a higher annual fecundity. The mass difference is already detectable at fledging, with male chicks growing faster and maintaining a size advantage throughout development. Field studies in the Philippines have shown that body mass can fluctuate by up to 10% seasonally, with birds being heaviest just prior to the breeding season when they accumulate fat reserves, and lightest during the energetically demanding chick-rearing phase. This sex-specific adult mass distribution has implications for the metabolic rate, with males expected to have a higher absolute resting metabolic expenditure.

The maximum lifespan of the White-breasted waterhen is estimated at 12.7 years [am = 12.7 years] when recorded at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], a longevity that is notable for a relatively small-bodied, high-fecundity bird. This figure comes from a long-term mark-recapture study in a stable marsh population and represents the oldest documented individual. Most birds in the wild do not reach this extreme age, with the average life expectancy being considerably shorter, likely between 2 and 4 years, due to high rates of nest predation, exposure to severe weather, and competition for territory. The basal metabolic rate of Amaurornis phoenicurus, measured as the maximum resting oxygen consumption at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], is 142.85 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 142.85 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. When standardized for body mass, this metabolic rate falls within the predicted range for a rallid of this size. The species’ ability to sustain a relatively low resting metabolic rate may be an adaptation for thriving in nutrient-poor or variable wetland environments, allowing it to survive periods of food scarcity without excessive energy drain. Comparative data from other tropical swamp-dwelling birds indicate a similar pattern of moderate metabolic expenditure.
